key_insight: Machine learning can distinguish palatal from epiglottic snoring using acoustic features alone, suggesting snoring carries a measurable signature of upper-airway obstruction site.
clinical_relevance: If validated, this non-invasive approach could help triage or complement DISE in obstructive sleep apnea by identifying likely obstruction anatomy from recorded snoring.
method: Retrospective analysis of 159 DISE recordings from adults with moderate, non-positional OSA.
Snoring events were labeled by two blinded experts, and only fully agreed events were analyzed.
Spectral, cepstral, temporal, and harmonic features were selected and tested with SVM and MLP models using patient-independent nested cross-validation.
evidence_signal: Using 1,759 snoring events, both models achieved ROC AUC 0.90 ± 0.03, with balanced accuracy of 0.83 for SVM and 0.81 for MLP.
watch_item: Results come from retrospective DISE audio with expert-labeled high-agreement events, so generalization to noisier real-world recordings and broader OSA populations still needs confirmation.
paper_title: The sound of snoring: AI-based acoustic phenotyping of upper airway obstruction in Obstructive Sleep Apnea
